name: Karl Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in the marketing office of a family-owned bakery chain. We've got about thirty shops and our bread is in the local supermarkets. I write the shelf signs, the leaflets, the radio ads, and the texts that go out on the loyalty card app, like 'Fresh doughnuts at four'. I've never used any of these AI tools. I do things the way Margit, my manager, showed me in my first month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's tiring?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The good part is it's a steady old firm. The owner's family has run it for three generations, and they don't sack people on a whim. The tiring part is that I'm not very quick, and Margit has to fix my spelling more than I'd like. The pay is low, my girlfriend Ana's a nurse and earns more than me, and I've got maybe three weeks of money put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's about what I thought. A few gadgets, some noise, nothing that changes how you sell a loaf of bread. I'd say that to the lads at football too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine with it. The bakery isn't going anywhere, and people will still want signs saying what's on offer. My worry is just my pay and that I'm a bit slow, not machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am and work on getting faster, maybe a spelling and grammar course at the library. I'd ask Margit if I could take on the radio ads fully, since that's the bit I'm decent at. And Ana and I would keep putting a little away for a deposit, even if it's slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled. A bit of the usual worry about money, but that's always been there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the bakery used a tool to write the app texts, would that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The app texts are maybe a fifth of my week. I'd rather they gave me something else than took the hours away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does saving for a deposit look like right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty a month, which is nothing. At this rate we'll buy a house when we're sixty. But it's a habit, and Ana says habits matter.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be **a few gadgets** and some noise.
I'd say it changes nothing about **selling a loaf**.
think: I think the **bakery** is steady and my job is safe.
My worry is my **low pay** and being slow, not machines.
do: Take a **spelling and grammar** course at the library.
Ask Margit to give me the **radio ads** fully.
Keep saving **forty a month** for a deposit with Ana.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with the usual worry about **money**.
S0.quote: My worry is just my pay and that I'm a bit slow, not machines.
fieldNote: He trusts the **family-owned bakery** to keep people on.
About a **fifth of his week** is app texts, the part a tool would touch.
Ana's **nursing pay** steadies a household with three weeks' savings.

steps.text: Ask Margit to hand him the radio ads fully
Take a spelling and grammar course at the library
Keep saving forty a month towards a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we'll have to see how the firm handles it. I wouldn't go on about it online, I'm not that type. At work I'd keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think they'd keep one of us in marketing, not three, and I'm the junior. Writing signs and texts is exactly what that card says goes first. I don't even know how to use the tools, so I'd be the one who looks behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Margit straight if there's another job for me in the firm, maybe in a shop, maybe as an assistant manager trainee. The family likes people who stay. I'd stop the deposit saving and keep it as an emergency pot instead. I suppose I'd learn the basics of the tools if they made me, but only then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit sick. I don't like change at the best of times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd learn the tools only if made to. Wouldn't learning early protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I've watched people chase every new app and get nowhere. I'd rather be good at what I'm good at. That might be a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be OK working in one of the shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I worked in a bakery shop at seventeen. It's early starts and the pay isn't better. But working in a bakery shop is real bread and real people, and nobody's writing that with a computer.

say: I'd say it's a **big change** and we'll see how the firm handles it.
I'd **keep my head down** at work and stay off social media.
think: I think they'd keep **one marketer**, not three, and I'm the junior.
Signs and texts are **exactly what goes first** on that card.
do: Ask Margit about a **shop job** or assistant manager trainee post.
Turn the deposit savings into an **emergency pot**.
Learn the AI basics only **if required**.
feel: Uneasy and **a bit sick**; I don't like change.
S1.quote: Working in a bakery shop is real bread and real people, and nobody's writing that with a computer.
fieldNote: He prefers to move **within the family firm** rather than learn the tools.
He admits refusing the tools **might be a mistake**.
His centre outlook means **no villain**, just how the firm handles it.

steps.text: Ask for an assistant manager trainee post in one of the bakery shops
Keep the deposit money as an emergency pot
Wait until told before learning the AI writing tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to get a grip, quickly, some kind of support for people who lose their jobs. I'm not political, but that seems like common sense. I'd say it to whoever asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be out of the office within months. AI doing any thinking work better than me, cheaper, is a short sentence for someone like me. The shops have about three years before the robots, so that's where I'd want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the shop side straight away, take whatever role there is, even back on the counter at five in the morning. Ana and I would cut back hard, no car, no holiday. And I'd lean on her wage more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. I keep thinking about what Ana would say if I'm the one bringing in nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ana say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say it's fine and we'll manage. She's like that. I'd still feel like a passenger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And in 2031, when robots could do shop work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know. I really don't. I'd be thirty-two with no skills anyone needs, and that's a sentence I don't like saying out loud.

say: I'd say government needs to bring in **support** for people who lose jobs.
I'd call that **common sense**, not politics.
think: I think I'd be **out of the office** within months.
The **shops** have three years before robots, so that's where I'd go.
do: Move to the **shop counter**, even at five in the morning.
Lean on **Ana's wage** more than I'd like.
feel: Frightened, and I'd feel like **a passenger** in the household.
S2.quote: I'd be thirty-two with no skills anyone needs, and that's a sentence I don't like saying out loud.
fieldNote: He grabs the **three-year robot gap** by moving to the shop counter.
He has **no plan** for what comes after 2031.
Relying on Ana's pay hurts his sense of being **a provider**.

steps.text: Move to the counter at one of the bakery shops
Sell the car and skip this year's holiday
Live mainly on Ana's nursing wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and firms like ours should look after people who've been loyal. I'd probably say it to Margit, quietly. Not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's the fast one again but with a bit more time to get used to the idea. My desk job still goes in 2031. The difference is I could move to the shops without it being a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to train as an assistant shop manager over the next year or two. Managing staff and rotas, talking to customers, that's more people than paperwork. And I'd keep the emergency pot going and maybe get it to two months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but not sick about it. More like dread on a slow timer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Shop managers do rotas and ordering, which is thinking work too. Have you thought about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I hadn't, to be honest. So the ordering bit goes in 2031 as well. I suppose I'd still be the one dealing with staff and the odd angry customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave the bakery firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not if I can help it. There aren't many jobs round here, and they know me. Starting fresh at a new firm sounds worse than staying at the bakery and changing jobs inside.

say: I'd say five years is fair warning, and firms should look after **loyal staff**.
I'd say that **quietly to Margit**, not online or in public.
think: I think my **desk job** still goes in 2031.
Five years lets me move to the shops **without panic**.
do: Train as an **assistant shop manager** over the next two years.
Build the emergency pot to **two months**.
feel: Worried, like **dread** on a slow timer.
S3.quote: Starting fresh at a new firm sounds worse than staying at the bakery and changing jobs inside.
fieldNote: He hadn't seen that **ordering and rotas** are thinking work too.
Loyalty and **few local jobs** keep him inside the family firm.
His plan rests on dealing with **staff and customers** in person.

steps.text: Train as assistant shop manager at the bakery chain
Build the emergency pot to two months of bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so there's no reason for people to get hurt if things are done properly. I'd say that's a job for the firms and the government together. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine in this one. Ten years is a long time. I'd likely be a shop manager by then, and the robot bit's another three years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in the marketing office a few more years while it lasts, then move across to the shops. I'd finally learn the tools, slowly, if everyone else has. Ana and I would go back to the deposit savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still a bit uncomfortable, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fine, but your office job still goes. Is that really fine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine-ish. Losing a job you can see coming for ten years isn't the same as losing it next spring. I'd have moved by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Ana change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for the house. Maybe a smaller one, further out. With ten years, I'd actually want kids, which I wouldn't in the fast one.

say: I'd say with **ten years**, nobody needs to get hurt if it's done properly.
I'd call it a job for **firms and government** together.
think: I think I'd likely be a **shop manager** by then.
Losing a job you see coming for **ten years** is different.
do: Stay in the **marketing office** a few more years, then move to the shops.
Learn the AI tools **slowly**, once everyone else has.
Go back to **deposit savings** with Ana.
feel: **Calmer**, with a path I can see.
S4.quote: Losing a job you can see coming for ten years isn't the same as losing it next spring.
fieldNote: He still expects to **leave the office**, but on his own timing.
Ten years brings back **family plans**: a house and maybe children.
He'd learn the tools only **after others have**.

steps.text: Stay in the bakery's marketing office for a few years
Move across to manage one of the bakery shops
Restart deposit savings for a smaller house further out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I'd have nowhere to go and no time to get there. What would help is the firm giving people like me first chance at the shop jobs, and some government money while we retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who just aren't quick. Everyone talks about learning new skills, but some of us take longer to learn anything. That's me.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about learning new skills, but some of us take longer to learn anything.
portrait: Karl is a **27-year-old** junior in a family bakery chain's marketing office, writing signs, leaflets and radio ads.
He has **three weeks** of savings and earns less than his girlfriend Ana, a nurse.
He avoids AI tools and prefers to **move within the firm**, towards the shops.
He goes from uneasy under AI Plateau to **alarmed** with AGI, and calmer with ten years.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **nowhere to go** and no time to get there.
whatWouldHelp: **First chance** at shop jobs inside the firm.
